reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive congenital enteropathy, most often caused by biallelic MYO5B variants, presenting in the first days of life with severe watery diarrhoea
The diarrhoea is predominantly secretory and persists during fasting, producing profound dehydration and electrolyte loss
Small-bowel biopsy shows villus atrophy with absent or shortened apical microvilli and characteristic intracytoplasmic microvillus inclusions on electron microscopy
PAS and CD10 immunostaining reveal abnormal apical accumulation of brush-border material within enterocytes
A milder late-onset variant exists, and some patients develop cholestatic liver disease reflecting the wider role of MYO5B in apical trafficking
Affected infants are dependent on total parenteral nutrition, and definitive treatment for intractable cases is intestinal transplantation
Antenatal or early genetic diagnosis is valuable given the severity and lifelong nutritional dependence
reference.pathophysiology: Microvillus inclusion disease arises from defective apical trafficking within the enterocyte. Loss-of-function variants in MYO5B (and less often STX3 or STXBP2) disrupt the myosin Vb-mediated recycling of apical membrane and transporter proteins to the brush border. The result is failure to assemble a normal apical microvillus surface, with brush-border components mislocalised into cytoplasmic vesicles and microvillus inclusions. Because functional transporters and the absorptive surface are lost, the intestine cannot reabsorb fluid and electrolytes, producing a severe secretory diarrhoea that continues even when enteral feeds are withheld.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital secretory diarrhoea from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Stool electrolytes and calculation of the faecal osmotic gap to confirm a secretory pattern
Small-bowel mucosal biopsy with light microscopy and electron microscopy
PAS and CD10 immunohistochemistry to demonstrate abnormal apical brush-border accumulation
Molecular genetic testing for MYO5B, STX3 and STXBP2 variants
Serial fluid balance, serum electrolytes and acid-base assessment during acute management
redFlags: Profound dehydration and haemodynamic instability from massive fluid loss in the neonatal period
Severe electrolyte and acid-base derangement requiring intensive correction
Failure of diarrhoea to abate on complete bowel rest, indicating a secretory process
Emerging cholestatic liver disease during long-term parenteral nutrition
reference.prognosis: The classic early-onset form carries a guarded prognosis with lifelong dependence on parenteral nutrition and its complications; intestinal or combined transplantation offers the main prospect of enteral autonomy. Milder late-onset phenotypes may be managed with prolonged nutritional support.
pitfalls: Mistaking the persistent secretory diarrhoea for infection and delaying biopsy and genetic testing
Attributing the picture to feed intolerance and repeatedly changing formulas rather than investigating for a congenital enteropathy
Failing to obtain electron microscopy, which is often required to identify the diagnostic inclusions
Overlooking parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis and catheter-related complications during long-term care
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Sustain nutrition and hydration with total parenteral nutrition, on which affected infants are dependent from birth
Meticulously replace the fluid and electrolyte losses of the secretory diarrhoea, with careful acid-base management
Prevent and manage parenteral-nutrition complications, including catheter-related sepsis and intestinal failure-associated (cholestatic) liver disease, through careful line care and lipid strategies
Offer intestinal, or combined liver-intestine, transplantation for intractable disease to achieve enteral autonomy
Monitor growth, nutritional status and hepatic function, watching for cholestasis
Provide genetic counselling and testing for MYO5B and related genes in this autosomal recessive disorder, with family screening
Coordinate a multidisciplinary team of paediatric gastroenterology, specialist nutrition and intestinal transplantation services
